title: Nambu Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics And The Lyapunov Structure Of Open Systems
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In open nonequilibrium systems, the thermodynamic entropy of a subsystem is not generally a Lyapunov function. Even during relaxation toward equilibrium, it may decrease temporarily because of exchanges with external reservoirs. This raises a basic question: what thermodynamic quantity, if any, organizes irreversible relaxation in an open system? We address this question using an explicit open-piston model coupled to both a pressure reservoir and a heat bath. The reversible sector is formulated as a Nambu rotational flow generated by the extended energy and the subsystem entropy, while the irreversible sector is written as a gradient flow generated by a dissipation potential [MATH]. In the adiabatic reversible limit, the Nambu bracket produces the oscillatory piston motion on the intersection of conserved level surfaces. After coupling to a heat bath and adding friction, the subsystem entropy [MATH] can exhibit nonmonotonic oscillations, whereas [MATH] increases monotonically under the proposed positive-semidefinite dissipative structure. We show that this monotonicity is not a consequence of identifying [MATH] with thermodynamic entropy. Rather, it follows from two geometric conditions: the reversible Nambu flow preserves [MATH], and the irreversible dynamics can be written as a positive-semidefinite gradient flow generated by [MATH]. The open-piston model therefore provides a minimal macroscopic realization in which thermodynamic entropy, dissipation potential, reversible temporal order, and irreversible relaxation can be separated explicitly.
tldr: This paper introduces a Nambu nonequilibrium thermodynamics framework for open systems, demonstrating that a dissipation potential can serve as a Lyapunov function even when subsystem entropy is not monotonic.
motivation: In open nonequilibrium systems, thermodynamic entropy is not generally a Lyapunov function, raising the question of what quantity organizes irreversible relaxation. The authors aim to identify a thermodynamic quantity that monotonically increases during relaxation.
method: The authors construct an explicit open-piston model coupled to a pressure reservoir and heat bath. They formulate the reversible sector as a Nambu rotational flow and the irreversible sector as a gradient flow generated by a dissipation potential, analyzing the geometric conditions for monotonicity.
result: The dissipation potential increases monotonically under the proposed dissipative structure, while subsystem entropy can exhibit nonmonotonic oscillations. This monotonicity follows from two geometric conditions: the reversible Nambu flow preserves the dissipation potential, and the irreversible dynamics is a positive-semidefinite gradient flow.
conclusion: The open-piston model provides a minimal macroscopic realization where thermodynamic entropy, dissipation potential, reversible temporal order, and irreversible relaxation can be separated explicitly, offering a new perspective on Lyapunov functions in open systems.

title: Unlocking Exponential And Unbounded Robust Gains In Shannon Capacity Of Classical Multiple Access Channels With Causal Csit Via Quantum Entanglement Assistance
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum entanglement assistance is known to improve the Shannon capacity of classical communication networks but the largest gains noted thus far are rather modest (less than 6%), motivating the question: are large capacity gains ever possible? It is shown in this work that in the presence of causal channel state information at the transmitters, quantum entanglement assistance provides a multiplicative capacity advantage that grows exponentially with the number of users K for certain classical K-user multiple access channels with fixed size (binary) alphabet for inputs, outputs and states. Similarly, in the presence of causal channel state information at the transmitters, quantum entanglement assistance is shown to provide a multiplicative capacity advantage that is unbounded as the size of the state alphabet grows, while the number of users (K=3) and the input and output alphabet (binary) are held fixed. Even with only a few users and small alphabet sizes, substantial multiplicative gains in capacity are found, e.g., with binary inputs, outputs and states, multiplicative gains by factors exceeding 21 and 88 are noted with K=5 and K=7 users, respectively. The gains are robust in the sense that they persist even with noisy quantum resources, e.g., an exponential (in K) capacity advantage from quantum entanglement assistance remains available even if each entangled qubit independently depolarizes completely with probability [MATH] 30%. The gains are based on quantum entanglement assistance provided only to the transmitters.
tldr: Quantum entanglement assistance provides exponential and unbounded multiplicative gains in Shannon capacity for classical multiple access channels with causal CSIT.
motivation: Previous studies showed only modest capacity gains (<6%) from entanglement assistance, raising the question of whether large gains are possible.
method: The authors analyze classical K-user multiple access channels with causal channel state information at transmitters (CSIT) and prove that entanglement assistance yields multiplicative capacity advantages that grow exponentially with K or unboundedly with state alphabet size.
result: For binary inputs/outputs/states, multiplicative gains exceed 21 for K=5 and 88 for K=7; gains persist even with noisy entanglement (e.g., 30% depolarizing noise).
conclusion: Entanglement assistance can dramatically boost classical communication capacity in certain settings, motivating further exploration of quantum advantages in network information theory.

title: Frustrated Superradiant Phases In One- And Two-dimensional Lattices
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how frustration and symmetry breaking shape collective behavior is a central problem in quantum many-body systems. In this work, we investigate this problem in large one- and two-dimensional arrays of coupled Dicke models on a periodic lattice, where strong light-matter coupling gives rise to a superradiant phase and competition between neighboring order parameters induces spontaneous translational symmetry breaking. Such Dicke lattice models constitute a fundamentally new class of quantum many-body systems, as they simultaneously realize the thermodynamic limit associated with the lattice size and an intrinsic thermodynamic limit arising from collective on-site interactions with quantum emitters. We show that frustration drives photonic density-wave ordering, and that the resulting broken periodicity can be predicted from the excitation spectrum of the symmetric phase, without requiring computationally prohibitive thermodynamic energy minimization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an emergent Nambu-Goldstone mode arises near the critical point in a one-dimensional chain despite the presence of only discrete symmetry, and uncover the mechanism that enables this otherwise forbidden gapless excitation. We also find quasi-periodic ordering in the superradiant phase, reminiscent of quasicrystals, and demonstrate that synthetic magnetic flux provides a powerful knob to control the nature of translational symmetry breaking. Our results establish a new direction in quantum many-body physics where the coexistence of local and global thermodynamic limits gives rise to unconventional symmetry breaking and emergent collective behavior.
tldr: This paper studies frustrated superradiant phases in Dicke lattice models, revealing density-wave ordering and emergent Nambu-Goldstone modes in one- and two-dimensional lattices.
motivation: To understand how frustration and symmetry breaking shape collective behavior in quantum many-body systems, particularly in arrays of coupled Dicke models where local and global thermodynamic limits coexist.
method: The authors analyze large 1D and 2D periodic lattices of coupled Dicke models using excitation spectrum analysis and thermodynamic energy minimization to predict broken periodicity and superradiant phases.
result: Frustration drives photonic density-wave ordering; an emergent Nambu-Goldstone mode appears near the critical point in 1D despite discrete symmetry; quasi-periodic ordering reminiscent of quasicrystals is found; synthetic magnetic flux controls translational symmetry breaking.
conclusion: The work establishes a new direction in quantum many-body physics with unconventional symmetry breaking and emergent collective behavior, relevant for hybrid quantum systems and superradiance.

title: The Score Hamiltonian: Mapping Diffusion Models To Adiabatic Transport
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We exhibit an exact correspondence between sampling with score-based diffusion models and adiabatic transport of ground states for a family of Schr\"odinger operators we call Score Hamiltonians, built from the learned score's quantum potential. We obtain novel density reconstruction bounds and principled annealing schedules via adiabatic theorems for Fokker-Planck equations with time-varying potentials. We find the fundamental limit of sampling is set by the ratio of squared score-matching error to Score Hamiltonian spectral gap - the inverse Poincar\'e constant of the data density.
tldr: This paper establishes an exact mapping between score-based diffusion models and adiabatic transport of ground states of Score Hamiltonians, deriving sampling bounds and annealing schedules from thermodynamic principles.
motivation: To provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for diffusion models by connecting them to quantum adiabatic transport, enabling principled annealing schedules and fundamental limits on sampling.
method: The authors construct a family of Schrödinger operators (Score Hamiltonians) from the learned score function's quantum potential and use adiabatic theorems for Fokker-Planck equations with time-varying potentials to analyze sampling.
result: They obtain novel density reconstruction bounds and show that the fundamental limit of sampling is set by the ratio of squared score-matching error to the spectral gap of the Score Hamiltonian (inverse Poincaré constant of the data density).
conclusion: The work bridges diffusion models and quantum thermodynamics, offering a new perspective on sampling efficiency and suggesting that adiabatic principles can guide optimal annealing schedules.

title: Programmable Spectral Symmetries In An Anisotropic Quantum Rabi Simulator
authors: Jia-Cheng Song, Yu Liu, Ming-Chuan Wang, Ke-Xiong Yan, Yang He, Yun-Hao Shi, Wei-Ping Yuan, Cheng-Lin Deng, Li Li, Zhen-Ting Bao, Yutao Chen, Xu-Yang Gu, Tian-Ming Li, Gui-Han Liang, Zheng-He Liu, Wei-Guo Ma, Zhen-Yu Peng, Shuai-Li Wang, Yong-Xi Xiao, Yi-Han Yu, Jia-Chi Zhang, Kui Zhao, Min-Xuan Zhou, Kaixuan Huang, Yu-Ran Zhang, Yu-Xiang Zhang, Zhongcheng Xiang, Dongning Zheng, Ye-Hong Chen, Kai Xu, Heng Fan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum Rabi model captures fundamental aspects of light--matter interaction, where symmetry dictates both spectra and dynamics. Over the past years, experiments have explored many of its nonperturbative properties, but have mostly focused on the isotropic limit, where rotating and counterrotating processes are locked together, leaving the broader symmetry landscape largely unexplored. Here we realize a programmable anisotropic quantum Rabi model in a superconducting processor, with independent control of the rotating and counterrotating couplings [MATH] and of a transverse bias [MATH]. Continuous anisotropy tuning, combined with a duality mapping, gives access to the full parameter space from the Jaynes-Cummings to the anti-Jaynes-Cummings limits. In the deep-strong-coupling regime, we show that anisotropy reconstructs the spectrum and turns complete collapse-revival dynamics into incomplete revivals even near degeneracy. With adiabatic state preparation and joint tomography, we resolve an anisotropy-induced ground-state parity switch, a crossing that has no analogue in the isotropic model. We further observe selective tunnelling associated with hidden symmetry in biased Rabi models and track its anisotropic displacement within the same device. These results establish a controllable route to engineering nonperturbative light--matter Hamiltonians, where symmetry, spectrum, and dynamics can be programmed independently.
tldr: This paper experimentally realizes a programmable anisotropic quantum Rabi model in a superconducting processor, enabling independent control of rotating and counterrotating couplings and revealing new symmetry-induced phenomena.
motivation: Previous experiments on the quantum Rabi model focused on the isotropic limit, leaving the broader symmetry landscape unexplored. The authors aimed to access the full parameter space from Jaynes-Cummings to anti-Jaynes-Cummings limits and study nonperturbative effects.
method: They used a superconducting processor with independent control of rotating and counterrotating couplings and a transverse bias, combined with adiabatic state preparation and joint tomography.
result: They observed anisotropy-induced ground-state parity switch, selective tunnelling associated with hidden symmetry, and incomplete collapse-revival dynamics in the deep-strong-coupling regime.
conclusion: This work establishes a controllable route to engineering nonperturbative light-matter Hamiltonians, with implications for quantum simulation and understanding of symmetry in quantum optics.

title: Emergent Self-Similar Quantum Revivals In Spiral Drives
authors: Xin-Chi Zhou, Liang-Hong Mo, Hongzheng Zhao, Bastien Lapierre
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We uncover a distinct form of nonequilibrium temporal order: self-similar quantum revivals in a many-body system driven by quasiperiodic spiral kicks, where the system recurrently returns close to its initial state at a hierarchically nested sequence of times. We demonstrate that both the fidelity and entanglement entropy exhibit this self-similar temporal structure. It originates from an emergent dynamical attractor, which we identify, such that all momentum modes eventually fall into the same closed orbits at self-similar times. We analytically justify this behavior and show that, for special momentum modes, this attractor arises as a consequence of a generalized spin echo process, and more generally we prove its existence using quasiperiodic SU(2) cocycles. Interestingly, the dynamics between consecutive revivals supports either volume- or area-law entanglement scaling, tunable via the driving parameters. In the presence of integrability-breaking perturbations, the system eventually heats up, but a long-lived prethermal regime with algebraically tunable lifetime occurs before heating sets in. Our results establish self-similar quantum revivals as a new paradigm for nonequilibrium quantum matter and provide a realistic route for its observation in current quantum simulators.
tldr: This paper discovers self-similar quantum revivals in a many-body system driven by quasiperiodic spiral kicks, revealing a new nonequilibrium temporal order with tunable entanglement scaling and prethermal behavior.
motivation: To explore novel nonequilibrium phases in driven quantum systems beyond conventional time crystals and Floquet engineering, particularly focusing on quasiperiodic drives that can generate hierarchical temporal structures.
method: The authors study a kicked rotor model with quasiperiodic spiral kicks, analyze fidelity and entanglement entropy dynamics, and use analytical arguments based on quasiperiodic SU(2) cocycles and a generalized spin echo to explain the emergent attractor.
result: They find that the system exhibits self-similar revivals at a nested sequence of times, with entanglement entropy showing either volume-law or area-law scaling between revivals, tunable by drive parameters. In the presence of integrability-breaking perturbations, a long-lived prethermal regime with algebraically tunable lifetime emerges before heating.
conclusion: Self-similar quantum revivals represent a new paradigm for nonequilibrium quantum matter, offering a realistic route for observation in current quantum simulators and potentially impacting understanding of information thermodynamics and quantum control.

title: Push-Pull Acousto-optic Modulator Based On Non-suspended Thin-film Lithium Niobate On Silicon Substrate
authors: Haorui Ni, Sunil Bhave, Mengyue Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Acousto-optic modulators (AOMs) are particularly attractive for microwave-to-optical conversion, quantum transduction, and optical frequency manipulation. For these applications, chip-scale AOMs that combine high efficiency, broad bandwidth, and low optical loss are highly desirable. Although suspended and resonant AOMs can enhance modulation efficiency, they typically suffer from stability concerns and limited bandwidth. Here, we demonstrate a non-suspended built-in push-pull AOM on a thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) on silicon substrate that simultaneously offers high efficiency and relatively broad bandwidth. We further investigate the orientation dependence of electromechanical coupling in X-cut TFLN by fabricating devices with different acoustic propagation directions and identify an optimized orientation for enhanced acousto-optic transduction. Our low-loss device achieves a half-wave voltage-length product of 1.004 V cm at 0.842 GHz with an interaction length of 400 micrometers, together with a relatively wide acousto-optic modulation bandwidth of 132.5 MHz. These results pave the way for efficient, practical integrated photonic-phononic links.
tldr: A non-suspended push-pull acousto-optic modulator on thin-film lithium niobate achieves high efficiency and broad bandwidth for microwave-to-optical conversion.
motivation: To develop chip-scale acousto-optic modulators with high efficiency, broad bandwidth, and low optical loss for applications in quantum transduction and microwave-to-optical conversion.
method: Fabricated non-suspended push-pull AOMs on X-cut thin-film lithium niobate on silicon, investigating orientation dependence of electromechanical coupling to optimize acousto-optic transduction.
result: Achieved half-wave voltage-length product of 1.004 V·cm at 0.842 GHz with 400 μm interaction length and modulation bandwidth of 132.5 MHz.
conclusion: Demonstrates a practical, efficient integrated photonic-phononic link, paving the way for quantum transduction and other applications.

title: Dissipation-coherence Tradeoff For Stochastic Oscillations
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous noisy oscillations in biochemical and mesoscopic systems require nonequilibrium driving and therefore dissipation. A striking conjecture by Oberreiter, Barato, and Seifert (OBS) proposes a universal lower bound on the entropy produced per oscillation period in terms of the coherence number of the slowest oscillatory mode. Here we derive a weaker but rigorous lower bound that preserves the OBS structure while introducing a mode-uniformity factor that quantifies how evenly the oscillatory eigenmode is distributed across states in the steady-state inner product. The result makes explicit that an eigenvalue-only prefactor can fail when the dominant oscillatory mode is localized. We also outline a proof-of-principle route for estimating this factor from low-dimensional data under single-mode dominance and sufficiently informative measurements, and derive an eigenvector-free corollary using only the smallest stationary probability. Translation-invariant Markov jump processes on a ring provide a symmetry-protected class with [MATH], so the refinement reduces to the OBS form; the drift--diffusion limit on a circle saturates the bound.
tldr: The paper derives a rigorous lower bound on entropy production per oscillation period in terms of coherence and a mode-uniformity factor, refining a previous conjecture.
motivation: To prove or refine a universal lower bound on dissipation in stochastic oscillations, which is important for understanding thermodynamic costs in biochemical and mesoscopic systems.
method: The authors derive a rigorous bound using the steady-state inner product and introduce a mode-uniformity factor to account for eigenmode localization; they also outline an estimation method from low-dimensional data.
result: A weaker but rigorous bound is obtained that preserves the structure of the OBS conjecture but includes a mode-uniformity factor; the bound is saturated in translation-invariant Markov jump processes on a ring.
conclusion: The work clarifies when the original eigenvalue-only bound fails and provides a path to estimate the bound from data, with implications for thermodynamic constraints on oscillations.

title: On The Cryptographic Structure Required For Verifying Qubits
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classically testing for the presence of anti-commuting operators on a quantum device is a critical tool underpinning recent progress in classical verification of quantum computation. While such tests can be based on cryptographic assumptions, known constructions rely on highly structured assumptions, e.g. trapdoor claw-free functions. In this work, we seek to explain this state of affairs by constructing strong cryptography from (certain forms of) classical tests of anti-commutation. In particular, we formulate the notion of a test of non-commutation (ToNC), an interactive protocol between a quantum prover and classical verifier in which the prover's final-round response is obtained by measuring one of two binary observables [MATH] depending on the verifier's challenge bit [MATH]. We prove that, for a broad range of parameters, ToNC implies classical-communication key agreement (KA), and ToNC combined with one-way functions implies oblivious transfer (OT). Along the way, we develop tools for and provide the first known results on hardness amplification for post-quantum KA and OT, where communication is classical but adversaries may be quantum. In particular, we prove the following results of independent interest. - Post-quantum hard-core measure theorem: For any efficiently sampleable high-min-entropy distribution [MATH] over pairs [MATH] such that quantum circuits have advantage at most [MATH] in predicting [MATH] from [MATH], there exists a sub-distribution [MATH] of density [MATH] on which [MATH] is nearly optimally quantum-hard to predict. - Post-quantum interactive XOR lemma: Given any classically-interactive protocol, if quantum adversaries have advantage at most [MATH] in guessing a private challenger bit [MATH], then two sequential repetitions reduce the advantage for predicting the XOR of the challenger bits [MATH] to at most [MATH].
tldr: This paper shows that classical tests of anti-commutation (ToNC) imply key agreement and oblivious transfer, and develops hardness amplification tools for post-quantum cryptography.
motivation: To understand the cryptographic structure required for verifying qubits and to explain why existing tests rely on strong assumptions like trapdoor claw-free functions.
method: Formalizes the notion of a test of non-commutation (ToNC) and proves implications to key agreement and oblivious transfer using new hardness amplification techniques (post-quantum hard-core measure theorem and interactive XOR lemma).
result: ToNC implies classical-communication key agreement; ToNC combined with one-way functions implies oblivious transfer. Also provides first hardness amplification results for post-quantum key agreement and oblivious transfer.
conclusion: The results show that classical tests of anti-commutation are cryptographically powerful, and the new tools may have broader applications in quantum cryptography and verification.

title: Gauging The Spacetime Code
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, the spacetime code has arisen as a candidate for a unifying view of fault tolerance in space and time. On the other hand, the recent study of dynamical phases has increasingly turned its attention to fault tolerance as a notion of a dynamically stable process. In this work, I explore one pathway between the two, achieved by gauging the spacetime code. This gives rise to a lattice gauge theory that inherits the elements of fault tolerance associated with a circuit, with Gauss laws corresponding to equivalence relations between configurations of spacetime errors and Wilson loops corresponding to detectors. The obtained gauge theory finds a surprisingly wide array of applications, from quantum error correction to condensed matter physics, and even learning theory: (1) It contains in its description foliated computation, and hence gives rise to one version of a gauge theory for measurement-based quantum computation. (2) For a class of topologically ordered mixed states, it gives us a gauge-theoretic language to describe the classical memory associated with the state. (3) The gauge-invariant observables of the theory which describe detectors also coincide with the learnable degrees of freedom of circuit Pauli noise.
tldr: Gauging the spacetime code yields a lattice gauge theory that unifies fault tolerance, measurement-based quantum computation, and noise learning.
motivation: To bridge the spacetime code framework for fault tolerance with dynamical phases and fault tolerance as a stable process, and to explore applications across quantum error correction, condensed matter, and learning theory.
method: The author gauges the spacetime code, constructing a lattice gauge theory where Gauss laws correspond to equivalence relations of spacetime errors and Wilson loops correspond to detectors.
result: The gauge theory encompasses foliated computation (measurement-based quantum computation), describes classical memory in topologically ordered mixed states, and identifies gauge-invariant observables (detectors) with learnable degrees of freedom of circuit Pauli noise.
conclusion: This work provides a unified gauge-theoretic perspective on fault tolerance, with implications for quantum error correction, condensed matter physics, and machine learning for noise characterization.

title: Information-Geometric Bound On The Robustness Of Entanglement Generation
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement generation is a central resource for quantum information processing, quantum networking, and quantum sensing. In practical implementations, however, entangling interactions are inevitably subject to uncertainty and fluctuations in the interaction strength. We investigate the robustness of entanglement generation in the presence of such imperfections and establish a direct connection between the robustness of entanglement generation and quantum Fisher information (QFI). For two interacting qubits, we show that the reduction in concurrence caused by fluctuations in the interaction parameter is bounded by the QFI with respect to the interaction strength.
tldr: This paper establishes a bound on the robustness of entanglement generation under interaction strength fluctuations using quantum Fisher information.
motivation: Entanglement generation is crucial for quantum information processing, but practical implementations suffer from uncertainties in interaction strength. The authors aim to quantify how robust entanglement generation is to such imperfections.
method: The authors theoretically analyze two interacting qubits and derive a bound relating the reduction in concurrence (entanglement measure) to the quantum Fisher information with respect to the interaction strength.
result: They show that the decrease in concurrence due to fluctuations in the interaction parameter is bounded by the quantum Fisher information, providing a fundamental limit on the robustness of entanglement generation.
conclusion: The work connects entanglement robustness to quantum metrology concepts, offering insights for designing more robust entanglement generation protocols and potentially extending to larger systems.

title: Tight Relation Between The Physical Effects Of A Quantum Measurement And The Information Gained About An Observable
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dynamics of quantum measurements defines a precise relation between the information gained about one physical property of a system and the observable changes in another physical property of the same system. Here, we express this relation in terms of the Hilbert space superpositions of the corresponding eigenstates and show how the probability of an observable physical change can be obtained from the Bayesian update of the probabilities associated with the information obtained in the measurement. Our analysis demonstrates that the superposition principle provides the tightest possible expression of the trade-off between information and back action in a quantum measurement.
tldr: The paper derives a tight trade-off relation between information gained about an observable and the back-action on another observable in quantum measurements, expressed via Hilbert space superpositions.
motivation: To provide a fundamental understanding of the information-backaction trade-off in quantum measurements, which is crucial for quantum information processing and thermodynamics.
method: The authors use Hilbert space superpositions of eigenstates and Bayesian update of probabilities to derive a relation between measurement information and physical changes.
result: They show that the superposition principle yields the tightest possible expression for the trade-off between information and back-action, linking the probability of observable change to the information gained.
conclusion: The work clarifies the fundamental limits of quantum measurements, with implications for quantum metrology, thermodynamics of information, and quantum foundations.

title: Engineered Dissipation For Faster Adiabatic State Preparation
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adiabatic state preparation is often slowed by nonadiabatic leakage near small spectral gaps. We propose an engineered dissipative protocol that uses a filtered reservoir to induce predominantly downward transitions in the instantaneous energy eigenbasis while leaving the instantaneous ground state dark. The leaked population generated by nonadiabatic driving is therefore continuously relaxed back toward the low-energy sector. An effective avoided-crossing analysis shows that in the regime where the engineered relaxation strength is much larger than the minimum gap, the runtime scaling can improve from the closed-system behavior [MATH] to [MATH] Finite-temperature upward transitions introduce a thermal error floor, but the enhancement survives when this heating rate remains below the target error tolerance. Numerical results show improved ground-state preparation over closed-system annealing. We also discuss a possible superconducting-circuit implementation using structured bosonic reservoirs.
tldr: Engineered dissipation accelerates adiabatic state preparation by continuously relaxing leaked population, improving runtime scaling from O(1/Δ²) to O(1/Δ).
motivation: Adiabatic state preparation is slowed by nonadiabatic leakage near small spectral gaps; closed-system protocols require long runtimes to maintain adiabaticity.
method: The authors propose coupling the system to a filtered reservoir that induces predominantly downward transitions in the instantaneous energy eigenbasis while keeping the ground state dark, using an effective avoided-crossing analysis.
result: In the regime where engineered relaxation strength >> minimum gap, runtime scaling improves from O(1/Δ²) to O(1/Δ). Finite-temperature upward transitions introduce a thermal error floor, but enhancement persists if heating rate is below target error tolerance.
conclusion: The protocol offers a practical route to faster adiabatic state preparation with potential superconducting-circuit implementation using structured bosonic reservoirs.

title: No-go Theorems On Simulating Uncertainty Principle's Signatures
authors: Chung-Yun Hsieh, Minjeong Song, Shin-Liang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty principle, one of the most iconic features of quantum mechanics, was originally viewed as a fundamental limitation. Since the inception of quantum information science, researchers began to use it to achieve quantum advantages. To better understand the origin of these advantages, an essential question is: To what extent can the uncertainty principle's signatures be simulated by a single measurement? As a single measurement clearly cannot demonstrate the uncertainty principle, such a simulation, if exists, implies the claimed advantages may either stem from other quantum features, or just be reproducible in a less resourceful way. In this work, we report a series of noise-robust no-go theorems, showing that strong enough signatures of uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even when assisted by quantum pre- or post-processing. This signature is modelled by complementary instruments. We completely characterise complementary instruments by a numerically feasible measure and show that they are necessary and sufficient resources for the advantage in an operational task that aims to unambiguously send classical information.
tldr: This paper proves noise-robust no-go theorems showing that strong signatures of the uncertainty principle cannot be simulated by a single measurement, even with quantum pre- or post-processing.
motivation: To understand whether quantum advantages attributed to the uncertainty principle can be simulated by simpler means, thereby clarifying the origin of these advantages.
method: The authors model uncertainty principle signatures via complementary instruments, characterize them with a numerically feasible measure, and prove no-go theorems that are robust to noise.
result: Complementary instruments are necessary and sufficient resources for the advantage in an operational task of unambiguous classical information transmission; strong enough signatures cannot be simulated by a single measurement.
conclusion: The results delineate the boundary between quantum and classical resources, with implications for quantum information processing and foundational studies of the uncertainty principle.

title: Single- And Two-mode Magnon Thermal Squeezing
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 01 June 2026;
tldr: Thermal squeezing of magnons is demonstrated in a ferrimagnetic insulator device, achieving noise below thermal levels.
motivation: To realize squeezed states in magnets for spin-based sensing and information technology.
method: Experimental demonstration in a ferrimagnetic insulator device, likely using microwave techniques to generate and detect magnon squeezing.
result: Observation of single- and two-mode magnon thermal squeezing, with noise dropping below thermal levels.
conclusion: This work opens avenues for quantum-enhanced sensing and information processing using magnons in hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quantum Radar Cross Section With Two-photon Entangled States
authors: Sunghwa Kang, Jihwan Kim, Zaeill Kim, Duk Y. Kim, Yong Sup Ihn, Su-Yong Lee, Sean Crowe, Stefan Evans, Marcio de Andrade, Joanna Ptasinski
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study two-photon entangled states for quantum radar cross section (QRCS), which is an extension of a single-photon QRCS formula. Since signal-idler entanglement does not provide any enhancement of the QRCS [Brandsema's PhD Thesis (2017)], we focus on signal-signal entanglement and derive the corresponding biphoton QRCS. We show that it can provide an enhancement over the single-photon QRCS and two-photon separable QRCS, where the performance is evaluated for various two-dimensional target geometries in monostatic/bistatic configurations. Furthermore, using the double-Gaussian approximation, we derive QRCS formula for biphoton states with arbitrary degree of entanglement and compute the resulting scattering patterns.
tldr: This paper extends quantum radar cross section (QRCS) to two-photon entangled states, showing that signal-signal entanglement can enhance QRCS over single-photon and separable two-photon cases.
motivation: Previous work indicated that signal-idler entanglement does not improve QRCS; this study explores whether signal-signal entanglement can provide enhancement, which is important for quantum radar and sensing applications.
method: The authors derive a biphoton QRCS formula for signal-signal entangled states, using double-Gaussian approximation to handle arbitrary degrees of entanglement, and compute scattering patterns for various 2D target geometries in monostatic and bistatic configurations.
result: Signal-signal entanglement yields an enhancement in QRCS compared to single-photon and separable two-photon states, with performance evaluated for different target shapes and configurations.
conclusion: The findings suggest that entangled signal photons can improve quantum radar performance, opening avenues for further research in quantum sensing and radar systems.

title: Continuous-variable Adapt-vqe For Bosonic Lattice Models
authors: Dimitrios Athanasakos, Gloria Tejedor-Garc\'ia, Jack Y. Araz, Mafalda Ram\^oa, Bharath Sambasivam, Sophia E. Economou, Felix Ringer
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a continuous-variable adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (CV-ADAPT-VQE). As concrete examples, we consider the ground-state preparation for (i) the Bose-Hubbard model and (ii) the bosonic Kitaev chain, including its extension with an on-site Kerr interaction. The former conserves the total boson number, while the latter conserves global parity. We construct symmetry-preserving operator pools tailored to each case and show, using GPU-based classical simulations, that CV-ADAPT-VQE results in significantly shallower circuits compared to Hamiltonian-based VQE approaches. Our results point toward direct applications in quantum simulations of condensed-matter systems, quantum chemistry, and high-energy physics.
tldr: CV-ADAPT-VQE uses continuous-variable quantum circuits to efficiently prepare ground states of bosonic lattice models with shallower circuits than Hamiltonian-based VQE.
motivation: Bosonic lattice models are important in condensed matter and high-energy physics, but their simulation on quantum devices is challenging due to the need for deep circuits. This work aims to reduce circuit depth by using continuous-variable adaptive VQE.
method: The authors propose CV-ADAPT-VQE, which adaptively grows a continuous-variable quantum circuit by selecting operators from a symmetry-preserving pool. They simulate ground-state preparation for the Bose-Hubbard model and the bosonic Kitaev chain using GPU-based classical simulations.
result: CV-ADAPT-VQE produces significantly shallower circuits compared to Hamiltonian-based VQE approaches while maintaining accuracy. The symmetry-preserving operator pools ensure conservation of boson number or parity.
conclusion: This work demonstrates the potential of continuous-variable quantum computing for simulating bosonic systems, with implications for quantum chemistry and high-energy physics. Future work may extend to larger systems and experimental implementations.

title: Thermalization With Gaussian Quantum Cellular Automata
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the long-time dynamics of many-body bosonic lattice systems under translation-invariant Gaussian quantum cellular automata. We formulate two sets of conditions on GQCAs which separately guarantee thermalization of any state on the local Weyl algebra to the infinite temperature state, whenever the state is locally normal and has uniformly bounded particle density. Our main intermediate result is a quantum many-body generalization of the classic Riemann-Lebesgue lemma which is a bound on expectation values of local Weyl operators involving their support and the state's particle density.
tldr: This paper proves that translation-invariant Gaussian quantum cellular automata thermalize any locally normal state with bounded particle density to infinite temperature.
motivation: Understanding thermalization in many-body bosonic systems is fundamental for quantum thermodynamics and information processing, particularly for assessing the long-time behavior of quantum states under unitary dynamics.
method: The authors formulate two sets of conditions on Gaussian quantum cellular automata (GQCAs) and prove thermalization using a quantum many-body generalization of the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma, bounding expectation values of local Weyl operators.
result: Under the specified conditions, any locally normal state with uniformly bounded particle density thermalizes to the infinite temperature state under the GQCA dynamics.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous criteria for thermalization in bosonic lattice systems, with implications for understanding equilibration in quantum information thermodynamics and potentially for designing quantum algorithms that avoid heating.

title: Learning Hamiltonians At Long Times
authors: Constantin Cedillo Vayson de Pradenne, Jordan Cotler, Hsin-Yuan Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of learning an unknown [MATH]-qubit Hamiltonian [MATH] from [MATH] for a single time [MATH], where [MATH] may be arbitrarily large. For broad families of local Hamiltonians, we prove that, with high probability over [MATH] and [MATH], any sum of local observables [MATH] that is normalized and orthogonal to [MATH] satisfies [MATH]. The Hamiltonian is therefore the unique approximately conserved local observable, and we can efficiently recover [MATH], up to scale, as the approximate null vector of a data matrix built from random product-state inputs and classical shadows. As a corollary, we obtain a weak equilibration statement: the infinite-temperature autocorrelation of every sum of local observables orthogonal to [MATH] decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount.
tldr: The paper shows that for broad families of local Hamiltonians, the Hamiltonian is the unique approximately conserved local observable, enabling efficient learning from long-time dynamics.
motivation: To understand the information-theoretic limits of learning Hamiltonians from long-time evolution, and to characterize the structure of conserved quantities in many-body systems.
method: The authors use random product-state inputs and classical shadows to build a data matrix, then recover the Hamiltonian as the approximate null vector. They prove that any sum of local observables orthogonal to the Hamiltonian decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount.
result: With high probability over the evolution time and Hamiltonian, any normalized local observable orthogonal to the Hamiltonian has expectation value at most inverse-polynomial in system size. This implies the Hamiltonian is uniquely approximately conserved.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous learning algorithm for Hamiltonians from long-time dynamics and establishes a weak equilibration statement, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and information theory.

title: Optimal Convex Approximation Of Quantum Channels Based On $\alpha$-affinity
authors: Liqiang Zhang, Chengling Fu, Liuyong Cheng, Guohui Yang, Changshui Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining the minimal distance between a target channel and a convex hull of predefined set of implementable channels is a fundamental problem in quantum resource theory, and provides key guidance for experimental implementations. In this work, we develop a unified analytical framework for optimal convex approximation of quantum channels based on the quantum [MATH]-affinity measure. We construct a channel distance metric induced by the {\alpha}-affinity and the ChoiJamiolkowski isomorphism, which satisfies the required properties of a well-defined channel distance. Subsequently, we present an optimization framework for the convex approximation of quantum channels, and derive analytical solutions for the optimal convex approximation of single-qubit unitary channels over both the SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families, obtaining closed-form expressions for the optimal parameters and the minimal approximation distance. This framework is further applied to the amplitude-damping channel, yielding the explicit form of its optimal approximation and the associated minimal {\alpha}-affinity distance. In contrast to conventional approaches based on the diamond norm, our framework provides a systematic and analytically tractable approach to quantum channel approximation under realistic constraints.
tldr: This paper develops a unified analytical framework for optimal convex approximation of quantum channels using α-affinity, providing closed-form solutions for single-qubit channels.
motivation: Determining the minimal distance between a target channel and a convex hull of implementable channels is fundamental in quantum resource theory and guides experimental implementations.
method: The authors construct a channel distance metric based on α-affinity and the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism, then formulate an optimization framework for convex approximation of quantum channels.
result: Analytical solutions are derived for optimal convex approximation of single-qubit unitary channels over SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families, and for the amplitude-damping channel, yielding closed-form expressions for optimal parameters and minimal distance.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic, analytically tractable approach to quantum channel approximation under realistic constraints, contrasting with conventional diamond norm methods.

title: Suppression Of Coherent Light Scattering In A Three-dimensional Atomic Array
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 02 June 2026;
tldr: Experiments with a three-dimensional atomic array demonstrate strong omnidirectional suppression of coherent light scattering.
motivation: Most studies of collective light scattering in atomic arrays have focused on one- and two-dimensional systems; extending to three dimensions is important for fundamental understanding and potential applications.
method: Experimental realization of a three-dimensional atomic array and measurement of coherent light scattering properties.
result: Strong omnidirectional suppression of coherent light scattering was observed in the 3D array.
conclusion: This work opens new possibilities for controlling light-matter interactions in three-dimensional atomic arrays, with implications for quantum optics and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Hong–Ou–Mandel Interference Of More Than Ten Indistinguishable Atoms
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 01 June 2026;
tldr: Demonstration of Hong–Ou–Mandel interference with up to 12 indistinguishable neutral atoms, showing multiparticle interference patterns with single-atom resolution.
motivation: Extending HOM interference to many massive particles is challenging; this work aims to observe multiparticle interference in a controlled atomic ensemble.
method: Experiments with up to 12 neutral atoms in an optical trap, using single-atom detection to measure interference patterns.
result: Characteristic multiparticle interference patterns observed with negligible loss, demonstrating indistinguishability and coherence across many atoms.
conclusion: Enables studies of multiparticle quantum interference and may impact quantum information processing and metrology.

title: A Class Of Multipartite Entangled States Based On State Transitions
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Transition states (T states), denoted by [MATH], as a class of multipartite entangled states characterized by a fixed number of state transitions between adjacent qubits. These states form equal-amplitude superpositions over all states with a specified transition count. Unlike Bell states based on two-qubit correlations, GHZ states characterized by global correlations among all qubits, and W and Dicke states based on fixed numbers of qubit excitations, T states are defined by transition counts along an ordered sequence of qubits. We prove that T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states through a chain of CX (controlled-X) operations, thereby establishing a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based representations of multipartite entanglement.
tldr: Introduces T states, a class of multipartite entangled states defined by transition counts between adjacent qubits, and shows they are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states.
motivation: To define a new classification of multipartite entanglement based on state transitions rather than excitations or correlations, potentially offering new insights into entanglement structure.
method: The authors define T states as equal-amplitude superpositions over all computational basis states with a fixed number of transitions (0→1 or 1→0) between adjacent qubits. They prove unitary equivalence to Dicke states via a chain of CX gates.
result: T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states, establishing a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based representations.
conclusion: The work provides a new perspective on multipartite entanglement but does not directly address the user's specific interests in information thermodynamics, quantum communication, or hybrid systems. The equivalence to Dicke states suggests limited novelty.

title: Feature Encoding In Quantum Machine Learning: A Survey And Practical Guidelines
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The encoding of classical data into quantum states constitutes the primary performance bottleneck in Quantum Machine Learning (qml) on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (nisq) devices. No existing framework jointly characterises resource cost, expressivity, and noise robustness, nor provides actionable selection guidelines for practitioners. This survey addresses that gap through a systematic review of 66 primary works (2017-2026) assembled via a PRISMA-adapted protocol across five academic databases. Four principal contributions are made. First, a three-axis cost-expressivity-robustness taxonomy classifies all major encoding families - basis, angle, dense-angle, amplitude, data re-uploading, and IQP - along independently measurable axes. Second, closed-form depth-fidelity bounds under nisq decoherence channels identify the critical gate-error rate p* ~ 10^-3 below which amplitude encoding is viable. Third, a unified treatment of Fourier expressivity, barren-plateau onset, and quantum kernel concentration as functions of the encoding circuit provides the first joint trainability analysis. Fourth, a five-regime decision framework maps (D, n, p, tau) - feature dimension, qubit budget, error rate, and task type - to a hardware-grounded encoding recommendation. The central finding is that for p >= 10^-3, shallow angle-based encodings consistently outperform amplitude encoding in practice, despite the latter's exponential qubit advantage.
tldr: A survey on feature encoding methods in quantum machine learning, providing a taxonomy and practical guidelines for NISQ devices.
motivation: No existing framework jointly characterizes resource cost, expressivity, and noise robustness for feature encoding in QML, hindering practical selection.
method: Systematic review of 66 works (2017-2026) using a PRISMA-adapted protocol, developing a three-axis taxonomy and deriving closed-form bounds under decoherence.
result: Identifies a critical gate-error rate p* ~ 10^-3 for amplitude encoding viability; shallow angle-based encodings outperform amplitude encoding for p >= 10^-3.
conclusion: Provides a five-regime decision framework for encoding selection based on feature dimension, qubit budget, error rate, and task type.

title: Optimizing Irreversible Perturbations Of The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm
authors: Qianyu Julie Zhu, Youssef Marzouk, Konstantinos Spiliopoulos, Benjamin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Irreversible perturbations accelerate the convergence of Langevin dynamics, breaking detailed balance while preserving the invariant measure. The design of optimal irreversible perturbations has been studied in the continuous-time Gaussian setting, but extensions to non-Gaussian target distributions, and the impact of time discretization on the design of optimal perturbations, have not been well understood. Numerical discretizations of Langevin dynamics introduce bias, which is typically exacerbated by irreversible perturbations; handling this interaction demands a joint treatment of acceleration and accuracy. This paper develops a systematic framework for optimizing position-independent irreversible perturbations of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA). We formulate a constrained optimization problem that simultaneously accounts for mixing efficiency and discretization bias, where the former is characterized by a spectral gap analogue and the latter is quantified via a weighted expected squared jump distance. Within this framework, we derive an explicit characterization of the optimal position-independent irreversible perturbation. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our design yields faster convergence with controlled bias, and improves mean squared estimation errors compared to other choices of irreversible perturbation.
tldr: This paper optimizes irreversible perturbations for the unadjusted Langevin algorithm to accelerate mixing while controlling discretization bias.
motivation: Irreversible perturbations can accelerate Langevin dynamics but interact poorly with time discretization, introducing bias. The authors aim to design optimal perturbations that balance mixing and bias.
method: They formulate a constrained optimization problem using a spectral gap analogue for mixing and a weighted expected squared jump distance for bias, and derive explicit optimal position-independent perturbations.
result: The optimal perturbation is characterized explicitly, and numerical experiments show faster convergence with controlled bias and improved mean squared estimation errors.
conclusion: The framework provides a principled way to design irreversible perturbations for ULA, with potential extensions to non-Gaussian targets and more general settings.

title: Symmetries And Overparametrization Properties Of Hamiltonian Variational Ansatzes For The $(1+1)$d $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Lattice Gauge Theory
authors: Kanta Yamanaka, Takanori Daiza, Katsumi Imaizumi, Yutaro Iiyama, Lento Nagano, Ryu Sawada, Koji Terashi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We perform detailed studies of five Hamiltonian variational ansatzes (HVA) based on the Hamiltonian of the [MATH]d [MATH] lattice gauge theory. The ansatzes are designed to respect local and global symmetries of the original Hamiltonian and therefore act on a finely segmented state Hilbert space. Following Larocca et al. (2023), we numerically study the dimension of the dynamical Lie algebra (DLA) and the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) of the ansatzes within specific invariant subspaces. The ansatzes all involve sums of weight-three Paulis in their generators, which is a feature that have so far been underexplored in this context. We also perform numerical experiments to determine the ground state energy of the original Hamiltonian via variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and observe that overparametrization of the ansatzes coincides with the apparent disappearance of local minima in the loss function, in line with the finding in the reference. Finally, the decay rate of the VQE loss function under gradient descent optimization is revealed to scale linearly with the number of parameters in the ansatz. These results help to enrich the theory of overparameterization of quantum circuits and inform the design of scalable variational ansatzes.
tldr: This paper studies symmetries and overparametrization properties of Hamiltonian variational ansatzes for (1+1)d Z2 lattice gauge theory, focusing on dynamical Lie algebra and quantum Fisher information matrix.
motivation: To understand overparametrization in quantum circuits and design scalable variational ansatzes for lattice gauge theories.
method: Numerical study of dynamical Lie algebra dimension and QFIM rank for five HVA ansatzes, plus VQE ground state energy optimization.
result: Overparametrization coincides with disappearance of local minima; loss function decay rate scales linearly with number of parameters.
conclusion: Results enrich theory of overparametrization and inform design of scalable variational ansatzes.

title: Reply To "Interpreting Bohm Quantum Potentials In `Computing Quantum Waves Exactly From Classical Action'"
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The recent arXiv posting arXiv:2605.20443 by Lohmiller and Slotine attempts to address the omission of the Bohm quantum potential in their proposed exact equivalence between classical action and the Schr\"odinger equation. They introduce a position-dependent time transformation to argue that the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude vanish for the Feynman kernel. A rigorous mathematical examination of this transformation reveals a violation of the multivariable chain rule. The spatial derivatives do not vanish in the physical reference frame. The mathematical framework presented by the authors remains identical to the well-established semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact exclusively for quadratic potentials.
tldr: This reply refutes a claim that a position-dependent time transformation can eliminate the Bohm quantum potential, showing the transformation violates the chain rule and the resulting propagator is just the semiclassical Van Vleck propagator.
motivation: To correct a mathematical error in a previous paper that claimed exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation without the Bohm quantum potential.
method: Rigorous mathematical examination of the proposed position-dependent time transformation, checking the multivariable chain rule and comparing with known semiclassical propagators.
result: The transformation violates the multivariable chain rule, so spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude do not vanish in the physical frame; the resulting propagator is identical to the semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact only for quadratic potentials.
conclusion: The claimed exact equivalence is invalid; the Bohm quantum potential is essential for exact quantum dynamics beyond quadratic potentials.

title: Time-frequency Analysis Of Nonlinear Compton Scattering Via Joint Probability Distributions
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The interaction of charged particles with an intense laser pulse gives rise to a number of characteristic spectral features of emitted radiation, including the generation of harmonics, spectral broadening due to the phase-dependent ponderomotive red shift, and the emergence of intricate sub-harmonic structures. These effects are accumulated over the course of the interaction with the electromagnetic field and are therefore inherently nonlocal in nature. For a deeper understanding of strong-field quantum electrodynamics (SFQED) processes and their practical applications, it is desirable to employ tools that enable simultaneous analysis in the time and energy domains. In time-frequency analysis, such tools are provided by joint distributions (JDs). In this work, we demonstrate how a JD can be devised within the SFQED framework. Specifically, we focus on constructing a non-negative JD, which allows for a clear probabilistic interpretation. We study the properties of the proposed distribution and test its utility by applying it to the nonlinear Compton scattering in complex laser pulse configurations with carrier-envelope phase and variable polarization.
tldr: This paper introduces a non-negative joint probability distribution for time-frequency analysis of nonlinear Compton scattering in strong-field QED.
motivation: To understand spectral features like harmonics and ponderomotive red shift that are inherently nonlocal in time, requiring simultaneous time-energy analysis.
method: Constructs a non-negative joint distribution within the SFQED framework and applies it to nonlinear Compton scattering with complex laser pulses.
result: Demonstrates the utility of the joint distribution for analyzing carrier-envelope phase and polarization effects in emitted radiation.
conclusion: Provides a new tool for time-frequency analysis in SFQED, with potential applications to other strong-field processes.

title: xCPS: An xAct Package For Covariant Phase Space, Noether Charges, And Entropy
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: xCPS is an xAct tensor algebra package for symbolic computations within the covariant phase space formalism of field theories. From a generic Lagrangian, xCPS automates the derivation of equations of motion and symplectic currents. It systematically determines whether an infinitesimal transformation in the space of fields is a Noether symmetry and computes the associated Noether charge. Additionally, xCPS can in many cases determine whether a tensorial expression is a divergence and, if so, find its divergence potential. By implementing vertical exterior calculus through a graded, supercommutative wedge product and vertical operators, the package enables efficient computations in gauge theories and higher-derivative models of gravity, including the derivation of thermodynamic quantities like Wald's entropy. xCPS is open-source under the GPL license and available at [URL].
tldr: xCPS is a tensor algebra package for symbolic computations in covariant phase space formalism, automating derivation of equations of motion, Noether charges, and Wald entropy.
motivation: To provide a computational tool for researchers working on covariant phase space methods, especially in gauge theories and higher-derivative gravity, where manual calculations are error-prone and time-consuming.
method: The package implements vertical exterior calculus with graded supercommutative wedge products and vertical operators within the xAct tensor algebra framework, enabling symbolic derivation of symplectic currents, Noether symmetries, and divergence potentials.
result: xCPS automates the derivation of equations of motion, symplectic currents, Noether charges, and Wald entropy from a generic Lagrangian, and can identify divergences and their potentials.
conclusion: The package facilitates efficient computations in covariant phase space formalism, aiding research in gauge theories and gravity, but its direct relevance to the user's interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems is limited.

title: Isospectrality And Operator Complexity
authors: Pradip Kattel, Yicheng Tang, Natan Andrei
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a pair of exactly solvable, isospectral fermion chains, one strongly interacting and one quadratic, that nevertheless display remarkably different phase structures and operator dynamics. A nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation maps one onto the other while preserving the entire many-body spectrum and converting local fermion operators into extended many-body strings. Thus, operators that evolve within a closed linear subspace in the quadratic model become interacting operators that generate increasingly higher-body terms and exhibit asymptotic Lanczos growth [MATH]. Despite their identical spectra, the two models realize distinct phases and sharply different notions of operator complexity. Our results demonstrate that free many-body spectra and interacting operator dynamics are fundamentally compatible.
tldr: Two isospectral fermion chains, one interacting and one quadratic, exhibit identical spectra but vastly different operator complexity and phase structures.
motivation: To understand how operator complexity can arise in systems with identical spectra, challenging the notion that free spectra imply simple dynamics.
method: Analytical study of exactly solvable fermion chains connected by a nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation; analysis of Lanczos coefficients and operator growth.
result: The interacting model shows asymptotic Lanczos growth and generation of higher-body terms, while the quadratic model remains within a closed subspace, despite identical spectra.
conclusion: Free many-body spectra are compatible with interacting operator dynamics, highlighting that spectral properties alone do not determine operator complexity.

title: Setting Angles In Quantum Approximate Optimization At Utility-scale
authors: Maosheng Guo, Joel Jurado Diaz, Anurag Ramesh, Conrad J. Haupt, Alberto Baiardi, Dimitrios Athanasakos, M. Emre Sahin, Oscar Wallis, George Pennington, Christian Arenz, Sebastian Brandhofer, Georgios Korpas, Ieva \v{c}epait\.e, J. A. Monta\~nez-Barrera, Jakub Marecek, Davide Venturelli, Stephan Eidenbenz, David E. Bernal Neira, Daniel J. Egger
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a powerful heuristic that seeks to solve combinatorial optimization problems using quantum hardware and classical optimization in tandem. Various methods exist to train the parameterized quantum circuits that serve as an ansatz in QAOA. However, which method works best to identify optimal angles for a given problem instance remains poorly understood, especially at utility-scale, i.e., [MATH] qubits or more. In this work, we address this challenge through utility-scale benchmarks from which we distill operational guidance for QAOA practitioners. First, we investigate approximation techniques, such as matrix product states and Pauli propagation, to find optimal angles. Second, we train QAOA on small-scale representative problems and transfer the angles to larger ones. We then validate the results on quantum hardware for utility-scale problem instances that can be meaningfully executed. In this way, we identify insights for QAOA angle setting strategies that work best for problems at the utility scale, including as a function of resource cost for the search. Crucially, the operational implications we draw from our benchmarks will help quantum optimization practitioners execute QAOA end-to-end pipelines efficiently on current and future hardware.
tldr: This paper benchmarks angle-setting strategies for QAOA at utility-scale (≥100 qubits) using classical approximations and angle transfer, providing operational guidance for practitioners.
motivation: To address the lack of understanding of which QAOA angle-setting methods work best for large problem instances, especially at utility-scale.
method: Benchmarked approximation techniques (matrix product states, Pauli propagation) and angle transfer from small to large instances, validated on quantum hardware.
result: Identified effective angle-setting strategies for utility-scale QAOA, with insights on resource cost trade-offs.
conclusion: Provides practical guidance for executing QAOA end-to-end on current and future quantum hardware, but does not directly address the user's research interests.

title: Multi-Qubit Dyadic Phase Fixing For Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation
authors: Justin Kalloor, Mathias Weiden, Ed Younis, John Kubiatowicz, Costin Iancu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires translating application-level quantum circuits into the Clifford+[MATH] gate set, where the [MATH] gate is the dominant resource cost. Phase kickback is an ancilla-based technique that can dramatically reduce [MATH]-count for rotations with dyadic angles, but has previously been limited to highly structured circuit families. We present Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), a general multi-qubit synthesis tool that extends phase kickback to general quantum circuits. DPF uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any input circuit. Combined with a decision matrix to automatically size the final phase gradient register, our end-to-end workflow achieves up to 70% reduction in [MATH]-count compared to and up to 60% compared to Repeat-Until-Success synthesis on a diverse set of benchmarks. We map these compiled circuits to a surface-code architecture to evaluate space-time volume, demonstrating up to a 60\% reduction in this metric as well. However, for some circuits and mapping strategies the two metrics diverge significantly, demonstrating that [MATH]-count alone is a useful but incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant program costs.
tldr: This paper presents a method to reduce T-gate count in fault-tolerant quantum circuits by extending phase kickback to general circuits via numerical unitary synthesis.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires compiling circuits into Clifford+T gates, where T gates are costly. Existing phase kickback techniques are limited to structured circuits, so a general method is needed.
method: The authors propose Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), which uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any circuit, combined with a decision matrix to size the phase gradient register.
result: DPF achieves up to 70% reduction in T-count and up to 60% reduction in space-time volume compared to baselines on diverse benchmarks, though T-count and space-time volume can diverge for some circuits.
conclusion: DPF is an effective compilation technique for reducing T-count, but T-count alone is an incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant costs; future work should consider other metrics.

title: Newton's Identity In Finite-Bead Fermionic Partition Function
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For non-interacting fermions in a harmonic trap, the partition function at any discrete number of imaginary time slices (or beads) and for any choice of short-time propagator admits an exact recursion relation derived directly from the contracted determinant form of the path integral. This finite-bead recursion is distinct from earlier continuum-limit recursions, which do not apply to the discrete time partition functions. By identifying a direct correspondence between this recursion and Newton's identity, application of a closed-form result from the theory of partitions provides an exact expression for the one-dimensional [MATH]-fermion finite-bead partition function. From this, the Thermodynamic and Hamiltonian energies and specific heats are analytically calculated for any [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and propagator choice.
tldr: This paper derives exact finite-bead partition functions for non-interacting fermions in a harmonic trap using Newton's identity.
motivation: To obtain exact expressions for finite-temperature properties of fermions in a harmonic trap beyond the continuum limit.
method: Uses a recursion relation from the contracted determinant form of the path integral, linked to Newton's identity, and applies partition theory.
result: Provides closed-form expressions for the partition function, thermodynamic and Hamiltonian energies, and specific heats for any number of fermions, beads, and propagator choice.
conclusion: The work offers a new exact tool for studying finite-time path integrals in fermionic systems, but its direct relevance to the user's interests is limited.

title: Decoder-Consistent Hamiltonians For POVM-Based Quantum Relaxations
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In compression-based quantum relaxations like QRAO, classical variables are encoded into qubits and decoded after optimization. We formalize that the choice of the quantum Hamiltonian is fundamentally determined by this decoder. By representing the decoder as a POVM, we define a unique decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via the pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value. Using this framework, we reveal that standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions, and we provide new approximation guarantees for the MaxCut problem based directly on POVM decoder design.
tldr: This paper formalizes decoder-consistent Hamiltonians for POVM-based quantum relaxations, revealing inconsistencies in standard QRAO Hamiltonians and providing new approximation guarantees for MaxCut.
motivation: To address inconsistencies in quantum relaxation optimization (QRAO) Hamiltonians for mixed-degree quadratic functions and to provide a principled framework for constructing Hamiltonians based on decoder design.
method: The authors represent the decoder as a POVM and define a unique decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via the pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value.
result: They show that standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions and derive new approximation guarantees for MaxCut based on POVM decoder design.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to design Hamiltonians for quantum relaxations, with implications for optimization algorithms on quantum computers.

title: Periodic Symmetry-Adapted Encoding: Qubit Reduction In Crystalline Electronic Structure
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the symmetry-adapted encoding (SAE) framework to periodic electronic structure, enabling qubit-efficient quantum simulation of crystalline materials. By constructing a [MATH]-point supercell Hamiltonian from a folded [MATH]-point calculation and systematically identifying all applicable space-group symmetry generators -- including spin-parity, point-group, and crystal translation symmetries -- we obtain qubit Hamiltonians with fewer qubits than the Jordan--Wigner starting point. We benchmark diamond, silicon, 3C-SiC, MgO, NaCl, CsCl, h-BN, wurtzite AlN, [MATH]-quartz SiO[MATH], and MgF[MATH] using active spaces chosen to preserve complete near-degenerate frontier manifolds across cubic, hexagonal, trigonal, and tetragonal space groups. Across the suite the periodic SAE removes 4--8 qubits. The B2 CsCl benchmark realises eight independent Boolean generators, i.e. a symmetry group isomorphic to [MATH], reducing CAS(6,7) from 14 to 6 qubits. This exceeds the [MATH] maximum of molecular SAE, where only two spin parities and at most three independent Boolean point-group generators are available, because the folded crystal supplies three additional half-translation symmetries. Noiseless UCCSD-VQE benchmarks against exact diagonalisation in the active-space sector show that the reduced encodings preserve the target energies to well below chemical accuracy while reducing variational parameter counts by [MATH]--[MATH] and CNOT counts by up to [MATH]. The largest circuit savings occur when translation and point-group generators act independently in the active space, demonstrating that periodic symmetry can be converted directly into both qubit and ansatz compression. The method is implemented in the open-source QuantumSymmetry package and requires no manual specification of symmetry generators.
tldr: This paper presents a symmetry-adapted encoding method to reduce qubit requirements for quantum simulations of crystalline materials, demonstrating up to 8 qubit reductions while preserving chemical accuracy.
motivation: Quantum simulation of periodic materials is resource-intensive; reducing qubit count is crucial for near-term quantum computers.
method: The authors extend symmetry-adapted encoding to periodic systems by constructing supercell Hamiltonians from folded calculations and identifying space-group symmetries (spin-parity, point-group, translation) to reduce the Hilbert space.
result: Benchmarked on 10 materials, the method removes 4-8 qubits, with the largest reduction (14 to 6 qubits) for CsCl, and preserves energies below chemical accuracy while reducing variational parameters and CNOT counts.
conclusion: Periodic symmetry can be directly converted into qubit and ansatz compression, enabling more efficient quantum simulations of crystals; the method is implemented in an open-source package.

title: Towards Stable And Accurate Electron Dynamics Via Neural Network Based Time-dependent Variational Monte Carlo
authors: Weizhong Fu, Zhe Li, Yubing Qian, Ruichen Li, Weiluo Ren, Ji Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time dynamics of interacting electrons lies at the interface between quantum mechanics and non-equilibrium physics, governing the microscopic origin of ultrafast phenomena of molecules and nano-materials. Though neural network variational Monte Carlo has achieved unprecedented accuracy for stationary state calculations, its extension to real-time evolution remains challenging. In this work, we introduce the neural basis time-dependent variational Monte Carlo framework, which achieves stable and highly accurate simulations of electron dynamics. By constraining the time evolution to a compact, customized manifold spanned by the neural basis, we effectively bypass instability issues and achieve long-term stable evolution. Moreover, we demonstrate that this framework yields benchmark-quality accuracy in simulating the laser-driven dipole responses of the hydrogen atom and a stretched hydrogen molecule, and accurately extracts the dynamic polarizabilities of helium and beryllium atoms. Our work reveals the vast potential of neural network wavefunctions for accurately describing real-time electron dynamics and establishes a promising new route for first-principles simulations of complex, time-dependent electronic phenomena.
tldr: This paper introduces a neural network-based time-dependent variational Monte Carlo method for stable and accurate simulation of electron dynamics.
motivation: Real-time dynamics of interacting electrons is crucial for understanding ultrafast phenomena, but extending neural network variational Monte Carlo to real-time evolution has been challenging due to instability issues.
method: The authors propose the neural basis time-dependent variational Monte Carlo framework, which constrains time evolution to a compact manifold spanned by a neural basis to bypass instability and achieve long-term stable evolution.
result: The method achieves benchmark-quality accuracy in simulating laser-driven dipole responses of hydrogen atom and stretched hydrogen molecule, and accurately extracts dynamic polarizabilities of helium and beryllium atoms.
conclusion: This work demonstrates the potential of neural network wavefunctions for real-time electron dynamics and opens a new route for first-principles simulations of time-dependent electronic phenomena.

title: Symmetry-adapted Qubit Encoding With Complete Active Space And Bravyi--Kitaev Mapping For Quantum Chemistry On A Quantum Computer
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space (SAE-CAS) for quantum chemistry on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors.
